handoff.purpose: SpineLedger class implementation with read-only mode, migration, transaction management, and intent recording/resolution.

symbols.name: SpineLedger
symbols.note: Crash-safe intent ledger over SQLite. Uses WAL, BEGIN IMMEDIATE, and internal lock.

symbols.name: SpineLedger.__init__
symbols.note: Initializes connection; in read-only mode uses URI with mode=ro, otherwise creates parent dir, opens connection, applies pragmas, and migrates.

symbols.name: SpineLedger._add_missing_columns
symbols.note: Adds missing columns like trace_id to intents table based on PRAGMA table_info.

symbols.name: SpineLedger._migrate
symbols.note: Runs _add_missing_columns, executes _SCHEMA statements, updates schema_version, and raises SpineError if journal_mode is not WAL.

symbols.name: SpineLedger.pragmas
symbols.note: Reads and returns actual pragma values from the database.

symbols.name: SpineLedger._txn
symbols.note: Context manager that executes BEGIN IMMEDIATE, yields connection, commits or rolls back.

symbols.name: SpineLedger.record_intent
symbols.note: Inserts a new intent row and an 'intended' event. Returns an Intent object.

symbols.name: SpineLedger.mark_completed
symbols.note: Resolves an intent as COMPLETED with optional effect_id and result.

symbols.name: SpineLedger.mark_failed
symbols.note: Resolves an intent as FAILED with an error string.

symbols.name: SpineLedger._resolve
symbols.note: Internal method: validates intent exists, checks for prior terminal event, appends event, returns updated Intent.

symbols.name: SpineLedger._append_event
symbols.note: Inserts an event row into intent_events.

symbols.name: SpineLedger._terminal_event
symbols.note: Queries the most recent terminal event (COMPLETED or FAILED) for an intent.

symbols.name: SpineLedger.get
symbols.note: Returns an Intent by id, or None.

symbols.name: SpineLedger.open_intents
symbols.note: Returns intents with no terminal event, optionally filtered by kind, ordered oldest first.

symbols.name: SpineLedger.recent_intents
symbols.note: Returns all intents (resolved or not) newest first, with optional kind filter and limit. Implementation incomplete in this chunk.

claims.text: One connection per instance. ``check_same_thread=False`` plus an internal lock lets a single instance be shared across threads (the loop's worker and a status reader) without two statements interleaving on one connection; separate instances on the same file are arbitrated by SQLite itself under ``busy_timeout``.
claims.why: The code uses check_same_thread=False, has an internal RLock (self._lock), and sets busy_timeout. It is designed for shared use.

claims.text: A READER MUST NOT WRITE. The normal path creates the parent directory, sets journal_mode=WAL (which writes the file header) and runs migrations inside BEGIN IMMEDIATE -- so merely OPENING a ledger to look at it mutates it. That is intolerable for callers whose whole contract is that they change nothing (the picker's --dry-run ranks a queue and must stay a read). SQLite enforces it here rather than this class promising it: mode=ro fails any write at the engine, so a future edit that adds one cannot pass tests.
claims.why: In read_only mode, the code opens with ?mode=ro and sets PRAGMA query_only=ON, which prevents writes. The comment accurately describes the design.

claims.text: HONEST LIMIT: opening a WAL database read-only still creates the ``-wal``/``-shm`` sidecars, because the shared-memory index is how WAL reads work. The ledger's CONTENTS are untouched (a test pins the file's sha256 across a read), but this is not "touches nothing on disk", and a genuinely read-only filesystem will fail the open -- which callers surface as an error rather than as a silently empty history.
claims.why: The comment honestly acknowledges that WAL sidecars are created even in read-only mode, and that a read-only filesystem will fail. This is a known limitation.

claims.text: journal_mode is persistent in the FILE (not per connection); the rest are per connection and must be re-applied on every open, which is why they live here rather than in _migrate.
claims.why: The code applies journal_mode=WAL (persistent) and other pragmas each time the connection is opened. This matches the comment.

claims.text: Bring a pre-v2 ``intents`` table up to the current column set. Runs BEFORE the ``_SCHEMA`` statements, and the ordering is load-bearing: ``idx_intents_trace`` names ``trace_id``, so on a v1 database the index creation fails outright unless the column exists first.
claims.why: The method adds trace_id column if missing, and it is called before _SCHEMA execution in _migrate. This ensures the index can be created.

claims.text: Driven off ``PRAGMA table_info`` rather than off the recorded ``schema_version``, because the two can disagree -- a database created by a newer checkout and then opened by an older one has the column without the version, and a version number is a claim about the file while ``table_info`` is the file. Ask the file.
claims.why: The method queries PRAGMA table_info(intents) to detect existing columns, not schema_version. This matches the claim.

claims.text: On a FRESH database ``table_info`` returns nothing (no table yet), so this is a no-op and ``CREATE TABLE`` installs the full v2 shape.
claims.why: The code checks if cols is empty and returns early. The subsequent _migrate runs CREATE TABLE statements via _SCHEMA.

claims.text: REPLACE, not INSERT OR IGNORE: a v1 file that has just been migrated in place still carries "1" here, and leaving it would make spine_meta lie about the schema the file now has.
claims.why: The code uses INSERT OR REPLACE INTO spine_meta to update schema_version, overwriting any previous value.

claims.text: A ledger without WAL loses the durability posture this module is built on; that must be loud, not a quietly weaker guarantee.
claims.why: After migration, it checks pragmas() and raises SpineError if journal_mode is not WAL.

claims.text: The durability settings AS THE DATABASE REPORTS THEM -- read back, not echoed from what we asked for. A pragma that silently failed to apply is exactly the failure worth surfacing.
claims.why: The method executes PRAGMA statements to read the actual values from the database, not from a cached variable.

claims.text: Every write runs here. BEGIN IMMEDIATE takes the write lock UP FRONT instead of on first write, so two writers never deadlock upgrading a read transaction (which returns SQLITE_BUSY without consulting the busy handler -- unlike BEGIN IMMEDIATE, which waits out busy_timeout).
claims.why: The context manager executes BEGIN IMMEDIATE before yielding, ensuring the write lock is acquired immediately.

claims.text: Call this BEFORE the effect.
claims.why: The docstring states this, and the method writes the intent before the effect is performed (as per design).

claims.text: ``effect_key`` is the caller's after-the-fact identifier for the effect (see the module docstring). It is NOT unique-constrained: a retried intent legitimately reuses the key, and the ledger records both attempts rather than hiding one.
claims.why: The schema does not have a UNIQUE constraint on effect_key; the INSERT statement does not enforce uniqueness.

claims.text: ``trace_id`` defaults to the AMBIENT one (:func:`envelope.current_trace_id`), which is why converting this producer required editing no caller. The sole in-tree caller lives in ``spine/attempt.py``; a run that opens ``envelope.trace_context()`` anywhere above it gets its intents correlated without that module knowing this feature exists. Outside a traced scope the value is NULL and the row is byte-for-byte what v1 wrote.
claims.why: The method calls current_trace_id() which is not defined in this chunk. The claim about callers and envelope module cannot be verified from this code alone.

claims.text: payload is re-read from the canonical text, not echoed: what the caller gets back is what a later reader will get back (a tuple stored is a list read), so no code path is written against a shape that only exists in the writing process.
claims.why: The method returns an Intent with payload=json.loads(payload_json), ensuring the returned payload matches the serialized form.

claims.text: Closes an open intent as COMPLETED. Rejects a second resolution.
claims.why: The method calls _resolve, which checks for prior terminal event and raises IntentAlreadyResolved if one exists.

claims.text: Closes an open intent as FAILED. Rejects a second resolution.
claims.why: Same logic as mark_completed; _resolve enforces once-only resolution.

claims.text: canonical_json before opening the transaction: an unserialisable result must fail without leaving a half-open write lock.
claims.why: The code calls canonical_json(detail) before entering the _txn context manager, so a serialization error occurs before any database write.

claims.text: Every intent with no terminal event, oldest first. This is the crash-recovery worklist: anything here either never had its effect performed, or had it performed and lost the acknowledgement -- the caller distinguishes the two by looking for ``effect_key`` in the world (see the module docstring).
claims.why: The SQL query excludes intents with a terminal event, orders by i.id (oldest first), and the docstring explains the purpose.

claims.text: Every intent, RESOLVED OR NOT, newest first. The read that closes the loop's return path. ``open_intents`` is a crash-recovery worklist and deliberately excludes anything terminal, so before this existed a COMPLETED attempt was reachable only by an id or an effect_key the caller had to already know -- which meant nothing could ask the ledger the one question a self-improving loop has to ask: *what have I already tried, and how did it end?* Without it the picker re-selects the same candidate forever (measured: five recorded gate-failed attempts left the top five of the queue unchanged).
claims.why: The method implementation is incomplete in this chunk (only docstring shown). Cannot verify the actual SQL query or behaviour.
